episode.title: Route shell substitution through reviewable permission decisions with visible warnings
episode.before: At parent commit 5ad5301805ef4aef2abc15596412c54e017c28eb, the permission manager and monitor tool could hard-deny commands containing $(), backticks, <(), or >(). In the permission manager, this happened only when surrounding rules caused full evaluation, so the same substitution could be approvable as a standalone command but denied inside a compound command with an unrelated matching rule. Hard denial also prevented YOLO-mode override. Some substitution shapes outside command AST nodes, and env-prefix substitutions removed by shell-wrapper stripping, could instead be misclassified as read-only and automatically allowed. Execution confirmations had no warnings contract or warning rendering.
episode.after: At a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113, substitution-bearing agent shell and monitor commands are treated as non-read-only and normally resolve to ask rather than an implicit hard deny, while explicit deny rules retain precedence. Detection covers raw and wrapper-stripped commands, AST substitutions in every statement-node type, and the regex fallback path. Shell and monitor confirmations attach a shared informational warning for substitution, and the CLI renders warning-colored, prefixed text while reserving wrap-aware terminal height so approval options remain visible.
episode.diff: Removed substitution-specific default-deny branches from the permission manager and monitor permission resolver; narrowed the manager's default result to allow or ask; hoisted AST substitution rejection above node-type dispatch; added pre-strip/raw substitution protection to shell permission and fallback read-only checks; introduced shared substitution detection and warning helpers plus an optional warnings field on execution confirmation details; populated warnings in shell and monitor call sites; rendered warnings in the terminal confirmation component with wrapped-row height accounting; and added regression tests for standalone and compound commands, all four substitution syntaxes, wrapper/env-prefix cases, explicit-deny precedence, warning generation/rendering, AST blind spots, and constrained layouts.

evidence_units.claim: The pinned implementation commit identifies the bug as an inconsistent, non-overridable hard denial of command substitution and states that explicit slash-command shell-injection checking remains out of scope.

The permission manager no longer calls detectCommandSubstitution to return deny from default resolution; default resolution now returns only allow or ask, with AST failures conservatively falling back to ask.

Permission-manager regressions prove that standalone, compound-rule, backtick, input-process, and output-process substitution resolve to ask, while an explicit matching deny rule still resolves to deny.

The shared hasShellSubstitution predicate checks both the raw command and its wrapper-stripped form; buildShellExecWarnings returns a common warning when either relevant representation contains substitution.
evidence_units.source: packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.ts, COMMAND_SUBSTITUTION_WARNING, hasShellSubstitution, and buildShellExecWarnings at a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113

evidence_units.claim: The shell tool checks the raw command for substitution before wrapper stripping, preventing an env-prefix substitution from disappearing before read-only analysis, and attaches generated warnings to execution confirmation details.
evidence_units.source: packages/core/src/tools/shell.ts, ShellToolInvocation.getDefaultPermission and getConfirmationDetails at a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113

evidence_units.claim: Shell-tool tests prove env-prefix substitutions ask rather than allow and prove warnings for $(), backticks, <(), >(), and raw-only env-prefix wrapper substitutions, with no warning for an ordinary command.
evidence_units.source: packages/core/src/tools/shell.test.ts, getDefaultPermission tests and describe('command substitution warning (issue #4093)') at a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113

evidence_units.claim: AST read-only evaluation now rejects substitution anywhere in a statement subtree before dispatching on node type, covering variable assignments and redirected statements rather than only command nodes.
AST tests prove substitutions in variable assignments, env-prefix assignments, redirect targets, and backtick assignments are not read-only.
evidence_units.source: packages/core/src/utils/shellAstParser.test.ts, describe('substitution in non-command node types (PR #4386 R4 regression)') at a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113

evidence_units.claim: The monitor tool removes its substitution-specific deny, relies on read-only analysis with ask fallback, and attaches the same shared substitution warning while preserving a separate Monitor permission-rule boundary.
Monitor tests change five wrapper and substitution cases from deny to ask and verify that confirmation details expose a substitution warning.
Execution confirmation details gain an optional informational warnings array intended to be displayed alongside, rather than as errors for, the command.
The terminal confirmation component renders each execution warning with a warning-colored prefix and subtracts its wrap-aware visual footprint from the command-body height budget.
CLI tests prove warnings render only when supplied and that a constrained compact layout truncates the command body while retaining the warning and all approval options.
evidence_units.source: packages/cli/src/ui/components/messages/ToolConfirmationMessage.test.tsx, issue #4093 warning tests and tight compactMode layout test at a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113

evidence_units.claim: The regex fallback read-only checker rejects substitution on the original shell segment before wrapper stripping, preventing stripped env-prefix substitutions from becoming read-only.
The commit records a wider successful sweep of 1,262 tests across 19 files and a clean strict TypeScript build after the final env-prefix fix.
evidence_units.source: git show a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113, commit message section 'fix(core): close env-prefix wrapper substitution bypass at L3 (#4386 R6)'

candidate_atomics.name: normalize-reviewable-shell-permission
candidate_atomics.title: Make implicit shell risks reviewable without weakening explicit denials
candidate_atomics.description: Remove a substitution-specific default hard denial so non-read-only commands enter the ordinary approval path, while preserving explicit deny-rule precedence.

semantic_action.intent: Produce consistent, user-reviewable permission outcomes for the same risky shell construct regardless of unrelated loaded rules or approval mode.
semantic_action.module_role: default permission decision policy for shell-like tool invocations
semantic_action.pre_state: A syntactic risk can produce an implicit hard deny in some rule-evaluation paths, while the equivalent command produces ask in other paths; explicit deny rules are evaluated separately.
semantic_action.post_state: The syntactic risk is non-read-only and resolves through ask unless an explicit policy rule returns deny; read-only commands may still resolve to allow.
semantic_action.validation: Exercise standalone and compound commands under relevant and irrelevant rule sets, alternate substitution syntaxes, sibling shell-like tools, and an explicit deny-rule case; expect ask for implicit-risk cases and deny only for the explicit denial.

candidate_atomics.name: close-substitution-classification-gaps
candidate_atomics.title: Detect shell substitution before lossy normalization and across the full syntax tree
candidate_atomics.description: Centralize raw/stripped substitution detection and ensure every AST node and fallback classifier treats substitution-bearing input as non-read-only.

semantic_action.intent: Prevent risky syntax from being silently auto-approved because normalization or partial AST traversal erased or overlooked it.
semantic_action.module_role: shell syntax risk classifier and read-only gate
semantic_action.pre_state: Wrapper stripping can discard substitution-bearing environment prefixes, and substitution checks limited to command AST nodes can miss assignments or redirect targets.
semantic_action.post_state: Substitution in either raw or unwrapped input, or anywhere in a statement subtree, makes the command non-read-only in both primary AST and fallback classification paths.
semantic_action.validation: Test raw-only env-prefix wrappers, wrapper-body substitutions hidden by quoting, assignments, redirect targets, backticks, and process substitution; each must be classified non-read-only and must not return allow.

candidate_atomics.name: attach-risk-context-to-confirmation
candidate_atomics.title: Attach a shared risk warning to shell execution confirmations
candidate_atomics.description: Add an optional warnings contract and populate it consistently for substitution-bearing shell and monitor invocations.

semantic_action.intent: Let users understand why a command requires review without representing informational risk context as a permission error.
semantic_action.pre_state: A risky command either fails opaquely or reaches confirmation without structured substitution context.
semantic_action.post_state: Confirmation details contain one shared informational warning when raw or normalized command input contains substitution, and omit the field for ordinary commands.
semantic_action.validation: Inspect confirmation details for all supported substitution forms, wrapped/env-prefixed input, and a control command; require one warning for risky input and no warnings field for the control.

candidate_atomics.name: render-warnings-with-bounded-layout
candidate_atomics.title: Render execution warnings without hiding approval controls
candidate_atomics.description: Display structured warnings prominently and reserve their wrapped visual height within constrained terminal layouts.

semantic_action.intent: Keep risk context and the user's available decisions simultaneously visible in normal and compact terminal layouts.
semantic_action.pre_state: Warnings rendered outside a capped command body can exceed the available height, especially after line wrapping, and push approval options off-screen.
semantic_action.post_state: Warnings render in warning styling with a prefix; their wrapped rows and separator are reserved from the command-body budget, whose height remains at least one row.
semantic_action.validation: Render warning-present, warning-absent, narrow, and compact fixtures; verify conditional warning visibility, command truncation under pressure, and continued visibility of every approval option.

candidate_workflows.name: replace-opaque-syntax-denial-with-informed-review
candidate_workflows.title: Replace inconsistent syntax denial with informed, policy-preserving review
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order workflow for moving a shell syntax hazard from an implicit hard-deny or accidental auto-allow state into a consistent approval path, with complete classification, visible context, and bounded confirmation UI.

workflow_graph.goal: Ensure a shell syntax risk is never denied merely by an inconsistent default branch or silently allowed through classifier gaps: it should require informed approval unless an explicit rule determines otherwise.
when_to_use: A shell-like tool has syntactic-risk checks duplicated across permission layers or sibling tools and equivalent commands receive different decisions depending on unrelated rules.
A permission fix that removes a hard deny could expose read-only-classification blind spots or lossy-normalization bypasses.
The approval surface needs to explain a risk while retaining usable controls in constrained layouts.
anti_goals: Do not weaken or override explicit user-configured deny rules.
Do not classify substitution-bearing commands as read-only merely to make them executable.
Do not apply the agent-tool approval policy to separately scoped user-authored shell-injection defenses.
Do not make warnings themselves errors or force ask when an explicit allow rule intentionally grants permission.
not_applicable_when: The syntax is prohibited by an explicit non-overridable product or sandbox policy rather than a default permission heuristic.
No approval mechanism exists and execution cannot be safely deferred to a user or configured policy.
The affected path is the separately scoped user-authored slash-command shell-injection path whose hard denial is an intentional prompt-injection defense.
inputs: All shell-like tool call sites using the classifier
Primary AST and fallback read-only classifiers
Regression fixtures for syntax variants, wrappers, explicit rules, and constrained layouts
workflow_graph.entry_state: A risky shell construct can be implicitly hard-denied in selected evaluation paths, or can evade review when normalization/classification misses it; confirmation does not reliably communicate the risk.
workflow_graph.exit_state: All in-scope shell-like paths classify the construct as non-read-only, default to ask rather than deny, preserve explicit allow/deny semantics, attach consistent warning context when confirmation occurs, and keep warnings plus approval controls visible.

steps.condition: The hard-deny removal depends on the read-only classifier being the safety gate.
steps.validation: Prove that raw-only wrapper prefixes, quoted wrapper bodies, non-command AST nodes, and fallback parsing all remain non-read-only.

steps.condition: An approval path exists and explicit rule decisions remain authoritative.
steps.validation: Standalone and compound implicit-risk cases return ask; read-only controls return allow; explicit matching denials still return deny.

steps.condition: The command reaches a confirmation-producing interactive shell-like path.
steps.validation: All supported risk syntaxes attach the shared warning and a plain command omits warnings.

steps.condition: The confirmation consumer is a height-constrained terminal UI.
steps.validation: Warning text, command truncation, and every approval choice remain visible in a tight compact fixture; warning-free confirmations retain prior behavior.

validation_ladder: Unit-test the shared raw/stripped detection and warning helper with positive and negative commands.
Test primary AST and fallback classification for assignments, redirects, wrappers, and every supported substitution syntax.
Test permission decisions for standalone input, compound commands with unrelated matching rules, sibling tools, read-only controls, and explicit deny precedence.
Test confirmation producers for warning presence and absence.
Render interactive confirmations under ordinary, narrow, and compact height constraints and verify both warning and choices.
Run the affected multi-package regression suite and strict TypeScript build.
stop_conditions: Stop if explicit deny precedence is lost or an implicit-risk command becomes allow through any primary or fallback path.
Stop if raw and normalized detection disagree without a documented, tested reason.
Stop if a confirmation consumer cannot represent the warning without hiding or removing user choices.
Defer surfaces governed by a different threat model instead of applying the agent-tool policy indiscriminately.
unresolved_or_deferred: The issue bundle lacks GitHub discussion, review, and status-check metadata; review rationale is available only through the pinned commit message.
The pinned commit intentionally leaves checkCommandPermissions hard-denial behavior for user-authored !{...} shell injections unchanged because that path has a distinct prompt-injection threat model.

Warning propagation to ACP and non-interactive consumers was explicitly removed as out of scope in the final commit, so this workflow grounds only the retained interactive shell and monitor confirmation surfaces.

unresolved_questions: The recorded 1,262-test and strict-build result comes from the pinned commit message; this extraction did not independently rerun that full validation suite.

Several changed CLI completion, directory-command, and provider files appear to be accompanying integration or branch-history changes and were not used to infer the permission-policy workflow because the inspected permission implementation and tests provide the direct resolution boundary.
